Therefore, this study aims to pro - vide a critical review of treatment methods and their application in the remediation of PFAS-contaminated aqueous matrices. Additionally, both individual and hybrid treatment processes will be assessed, with a particular focus on the role of MSP as a key process in the development of composite technologies for PFAS remediation. Existing reviews have emphasized either emerging membrane ma - terials without systematically discussing the commercially available ones or focused primarily on high-pressure separations (nanofiltration and reverse osmosis [21] ) without integrating modified micro- and ul - trafiltration or downstream concentrate handling. A review centered on mixed-matrix membranes have additionally been scoped to wastewater applications [22] . In contrast, the present review consolidates perfor - mance data for commercially available and modified membranes and interprets rejection efficiency under environmentally relevant matrices (surface water vs. groundwater), accounting for natural organic matter, divalent cations, ionic strength, and fouling/adsorption mechanisms. It further links upstream separation performance to concentrate-management options and integration with destructive pro - cesses, enabling a coherent view of treatment trains rather than isolated unit operations. In brief, MF and UF membranes are porous media capable of retaining suspended solids and macromole - cules. They operate at lower pressures and, consequently, have lower energy requirements. However, they exhibit limited PFAS rejection, which occurs mainly through adsorption onto the membrane matrix. NF offers higher PFAS retention efficiency, particularly for long-chain PFAS. Finally, RO is expected to provide the highest rejection among all processes mentioned. It uses a non-porous membrane, and separation is based on the different diffusion capacities of water and contaminants through the polymeric matrix under hydraulic pressure. PFAS removal using NF and RO membranes is intricately influenced by several factors. These include the physiochemical properties of PFAS, the inherent characteristics of the membrane, and the influent water conditions. Firstly, the structural characteristics of PFAS play a signifi - cant role in the removal process. PFAS typically consist of perfluorinated alkyl chains, with molecular weights ranging from several hundred to several thousand, depending on their chemical structure and chain length. Consequently, the removal efficiency through membrane sepa - ration processes varies significantly, generally exhibiting higher removal rates for high-molecular-weight PFAS [18 , 19] . Secondly, the inherent characteristics of the membrane, such as pore size and surface properties of the membrane material, also have a profound impact on the removal efficiency of PFAS. In addition to the pore size of the membrane affecting the size-exclusion effect on PFAS, the hydro - philicity/hydrophobicity of the membrane surface and the surface charge also influence the interaction between the membrane and PFAS molecules, thereby affecting the final rejection rate [20 – 22] . This effect is particularly pronounced in the process of NF separation processes of PFAS. Finally, the influent conditions, including the concentration of PFAS, pH value, concentration of inorganic ions, and operation pressure, among others, directly influence the membrane performance and PFAS removal efficiency.
